```{r, load libraries} 
#| output: FALSE

#loading libraries

library(tidyverse)
library(psych)
library(patchwork)
library(janitor)
library(ggthemes)
library(gt)
```

```{r, import files}
#| output: FALSE

#Load data
Complete_ADHD_Knowledge <- read_csv("./Complete_ADHD_Knowledge.csv", na = "NA")

```

```{r, clean data}
#|output: FALSE
#Removing people who didn't answer anything
Complete_ADHD_Knowledge <- Complete_ADHD_Knowledge |>   
  filter(Knowledge_Total > 0)

#Removing countries with n < 20 for each role
Complete_Knowledge_high_n <- Complete_ADHD_Knowledge |> 
  group_by(Country_Residence) |> 
  filter(!(Role %in% "teacher" & sum(Role %in% "teacher") < 20),
         !(Role %in% "parent"  & sum(Role %in% "parent")  < 20)) |> 
  ungroup()
```

```{r, academic visuals}
#|output: FALSE
#Figure 1: T&T parents vs teachers

fig1 <- Complete_Knowledge_high_n |> 
  filter(Country_Residence == "Trinidad & Tobago") |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = Role, y = Knowledge_Corr_Percent)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "summary", fun = "mean",
           fill = "grey75", width = 0.6) +                  
  stat_summary(geom = "errorbar", fun.data = mean_cl_normal,
               width = 0.2, linewidth = 0.6) +              
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c(parent = "Parent", teacher = "Teacher")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 80)) +                        
  theme_hc() +
  labs(title = "ADHD Knowledge: Trinidad & Tobago",
       x = NULL, y = "ADHD Knowledge: % Correct") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 13),                  
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11)
  )

#Figure 2: T&T with Canada comparisons
fig2 <- Complete_Knowledge_high_n |> 
  filter(Country_Residence %in% c("Trinidad & Tobago", "Canada"),
         Data_source == "Ronald") |>                        #NOTE: Canada's means differ slightly from Figs 3-4 because of this filter
  mutate(Country_Residence = factor(Country_Residence,      #Done to show my original comparisons, before Canada observations from Tyler's data
                                    levels = c("Trinidad & Tobago", "Canada"))) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = Country_Residence, y = Knowledge_Corr_Percent)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "summary", fun = "mean",
           fill = "grey75", width = 0.7) +                  
  stat_summary(geom = "errorbar", fun.data = mean_cl_normal,
               width = 0.2, linewidth = 0.6) +              
  facet_wrap(~Role,
             labeller = labeller(Role = c(parent = "Parent", teacher = "Teacher"))) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 80)) +                       
  theme_hc() +
  labs(title = "ADHD Knowledge: Trinidad & Tobago and Canada",
       x = NULL, y = "ADHD Knowledge: % Correct") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 12),                  
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11),
    strip.background = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
    panel.spacing = unit(1.5, "lines")   #Better visual than default                   
  )

#Figure 3: Parents, all countries
fig3 <- Complete_Knowledge_high_n |> 
  filter(Role == "parent") |> 
  mutate(Country_Residence = fct_reorder(Country_Residence, Knowledge_Corr_Percent,
                                         .fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = Country_Residence, y = Knowledge_Corr_Percent)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "summary", fun = "mean",
           fill = "grey75", width = 0.8) +                  
  stat_summary(geom = "errorbar", fun.data = mean_cl_normal,
               width = 0.3, linewidth = 0.6) +              
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 80)) +                       
  theme_hc() +
  labs(title = "Parent ADHD Knowledge",
       x = NULL, y = "ADHD Knowledge: % Correct") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 12),  
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11),
    plot.margin = margin(5.5, 5.5, 5.5, 40)
  )

#Figure 4: Teachers, all countries
fig4 <- Complete_Knowledge_high_n |> 
  filter(Role == "teacher") |> 
  mutate(Country_Residence = fct_reorder(Country_Residence, Knowledge_Corr_Percent,
                                         .fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = Country_Residence, y = Knowledge_Corr_Percent)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "summary", fun = "mean",
           fill = "grey75", width = 0.8) +                  # CHANGED: light fill
  stat_summary(geom = "errorbar", fun.data = mean_cl_normal,
               width = 0.3, linewidth = 0.6) +              # CHANGED: thinner lines
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 80)) +                        # CHANGED: same range as Fig 3
  theme_hc() +
  labs(title = "Teacher ADHD Knowledge",
       x = NULL, y = "ADHD Knowledge: % Correct") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 12),  # CHANGED: bigger labels
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11)
  )

#Figure 5: Parents and teachers, all countries (patchwork)
#Intermediate figs 3 & 4
fig3_comb <- fig3 +
  labs(title = "Parents") +                                 
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    plot.margin = margin(5.5, 5.5, 5.5, 25)                 #Extra left margin so "Trinidad & Tobago" isn't clipped
  )

fig4_comb <- fig4 +
  labs(title = "Teachers", y = NULL) +                      #No y title (shared with parent panel)
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),                          #Hide y-axis; both panels share 0-80
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank()
  )

fig5 <- (fig3_comb | fig4_comb) +                           
  plot_layout(widths = c(14.5, 8)) +    #Setting panel widths to account for different number of countries in parent and teacher figures
  plot_annotation(
    title = "ADHD Knowledge by Country",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5))
  )

```

```{r, academic tables and misc objects}
#|output: FALSE

#Table 1: Country means
means_tab <- Complete_Knowledge_high_n |> 
  mutate(Country_Residence = fct_reorder(Country_Residence, Knowledge_Corr_Percent,
                                         .fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)) |> 
  tabyl(Country_Residence, Role) |> 
  adorn_totals(where = c("col", "row"))

means_gt <- means_tab |> 
  gt() |> 
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Table 1**"),
    subtitle = md("*Sample size by country and role*")
  ) |> 
  cols_label(
    Country_Residence = "Country",
    parent  = "Parents",
    teacher = "Teachers",
    Total   = "Total"
  ) |> 
  tab_spanner(label = "Participants", columns = c(parent, teacher, Total)) |> 
  fmt_number(columns = c(parent, teacher, Total), decimals = 0, use_seps = TRUE) |> 
  sub_zero(columns = c(parent, teacher), zero_text = "–") |> 
  cols_align(align = "left",   columns = Country_Residence) |> 
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = c(parent, teacher, Total)) |> 
  # Bold column labels
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) |> 
  # Bold, shaded totals row
  tab_style(
    style = list(cell_text(weight = "bold"), cell_fill(color = "grey92")),
    locations = cells_body(rows = Country_Residence == "Total")
  ) |> 
  # Bold totals column
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = Total)
  ) |> 
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Note. Countries are ordered by overall mean ADHD knowledge score (lowest to highest). Dashes indicate no participants in that role."
  ) |> 
  opt_table_font(font = google_font("Source Sans Pro")) |> 
  tab_options(
    table.border.top.style = "solid",
    table.border.top.color = "black",
    table.border.bottom.color = "black",
    column_labels.border.bottom.color = "black",
    heading.align = "left",
    data_row.padding = px(4)
  ) 

#Original sample size
n_TT_Can <- Complete_Knowledge_high_n |> 
  filter(Country_Residence %in% c("Trinidad & Tobago", "Canada") & Data_source == "Ronald") |> 
  nrow()

#Number of countries
n_countries <- n_distinct(Complete_ADHD_Knowledge$Country_Residence, na.rm = TRUE)

#Total number of participants
n_participants <- nrow(Complete_ADHD_Knowledge)

n_TT_participants <- Complete_ADHD_Knowledge |> 
  filter(Country_Residence == "Trinidad & Tobago") |> 
  nrow()

n_Can_participants <- Complete_ADHD_Knowledge |> 
  filter(Country_Residence == "Canada") |> 
  nrow()

#T&T percentages
M_TT_parent <- Complete_Knowledge_high_n |> 
  filter(Country_Residence == "Trinidad & Tobago", Role == "parent") |> 
  summarise(M = round(mean(Knowledge_Corr_Percent, na.rm = TRUE), 2)) |> 
  pull(M)

M_TT_teacher <- Complete_Knowledge_high_n |> 
  filter(Country_Residence == "Trinidad & Tobago", Role == "teacher") |> 
  summarise(M = round(mean(Knowledge_Corr_Percent, na.rm = TRUE), 2)) |> 
  pull(M)
```

# Story Summary
In Trinidad & Tobago, as elsewhere in Latin America and the Caribbean, Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is thought to be widely undiagnosed and undertreated, placing affected children at risk of negative outcomes. Although the literature identifies this regional phenomenon as problematic, its underlying dynamics remain unclear.
Our previous study examined factors that may contribute to undiagnosed and undertreated ADHD in Trinidad & Tobago. Compared with Canadians, Trinidadian and Tobagonian parents and teachers were more likely to attribute ADHD-related behaviours to indiscipline or low motivation. They also demonstrated markedly less ADHD-specific knowledge.
However, Canada is considered highly receptive to biomedical interpretations of children’s atypical behaviours. Consequently, our initial comparison could not establish whether ADHD-specific knowledge in Trinidad & Tobago was low in a broad sense, or merely lower than in a highly medicalized country.
The current study addresses this limitation by comparing ADHD-specific knowledge among Trinidadian and Tobagonian parents and teachers with knowledge reported in other countries. To make this comparison, we combined our data with comparable data collected by researchers at RMIT University. Preliminary findings indicate that Trinidad and Tobago had the lowest parent and teacher knowledge scores among all sampled countries. Further inferential analyses will determine whether these differences are statistically significant.

# Version A: Scientific Article
Trinidad & Tobago is located in the Latin America and Caribbean region, where ADHD is thought to be disproportionately undiagnosed and undertreated among children. Unrecognized of mischaracterized symptoms may be a contributor to this phenomenon; parents and teachers in Trinidad & Tobago were found to interpret ADHD-related behaviours as indiscipline and low motivation, more so than Canadians. In our previous study, we also found that factual knowledge about ADHD was markedly lower among participants from Trinidad & Tobago, versus participants from Canada. 
As seen in Figures 1 and 2, ADHD knowledge (measured by percentage of correct responses on the ADHD Knowledge Questionnaire), was significantly lower among parents (*M* = ; *t*(df) , *p* = ) and teachers (*M* = ; *t*(df) , *p* = ). 
```{r}
fig1
```

```{r}
fig2
```
It is appealing to infer that ADHD in Trinidad & Tobago goes undiagnosed beacuse its symptoms go unrecognized, itself a product of low knowldege. while appealing, these causal inferences are tenuous for multiple reasons, one of which relates to "low knowledge". Our results indicate that Trinidad & Tobago's ADHD knowledge was *lower* than Canada's, but this contrast may be misleading. 
Especially in terms of ADHD, Canada is thought to be a highly medicalized society, fluent and au courant with biomedical interpretations of atypical behaviours in children. It is therefore unclear whether ADHD knowledge in Trinidad & Tobago is *particularly* low, or only appears as such in contrast to Canada. As such, the present study is geared toward contextualizing ADHD knowledge in Trinidad & Tobago, against the backdrop of a broader cross-section of countries. 

# Methods

## Data
We analyzed data from our original dataset of parents and teachers from Trinidad & Tobago and Canada, (*n* = `{r} n_TT_Can`), in combination with data collected by researchers at RMIT University, from `{r} n_countries` countries. Our combined dataset originally comprised *n* = `{r} n_participants`. After removing countries with <20 parents or teachers, our reduced dataset comprised participants as delineated in Table 1.

```{r}
means_gt

```

## Instrument and Analysis
All participants completed the ADHD Knowledge Questionnaire (AKQ), developed by Kos et al. (2004). The version used in our original study was adopted from Youssef et al. (2015) and comprised 26 items (True/False, "I don't know"). The RMIT version comprised the original 27 items. The only substantive difference between the two versions was item 26 from the original ("Research has shown that prolonged use of stimulant medications leads to increased addiction (i.e., drug, alcohol) in adulthood"). For the present study, we computed the percentage of correct responses on the 26 items common to both prior analyses. Missing items were not imputed.
All current analyses were conducted in R, version 4.6.0, using the following packages: `tidyverse`, `psych`, `patchwork`, `janitor`, `ggthemes` and `gt`. 

# Results
```{r}
fig3
```
As seen in Figure 3, mean ADHD knowledge in Trinidad & Tobago was the lowest among all countries sampled, for both parents (*M* = `{r} M_TT_parent`) and teachers (*M* = `{r} M_TT_teacher`). 

#Conclusion
Initial descriptive statistics suggest that factual knowledge about ADHD in Trinidad & Tobago is low in comparison with a broader cross-section of countries. Further inferential tests will be conducted to determine whether preliminary findings are statistically significant.  

# Accessible/Dynamic Outlet Version
In Trinidad & Tobago, children with ADHD can often end up without the supports they need, because their parents and teachers don't recognize their symptoms. 

If the adults in their lives don't know about ADHD, they won't be able to recognize children's symptoms. 

Right now, it isn't clear how much parents and teachers in Trinidad & Tobago know about ADHD. 
That's why we decided to measure it. 

We asked `{r} n_TT_participants` parents and teachers 26 questions about ADHD. Here's how they performed on average:
```{r}
p_TT_only
```
`{r} M_TT_parent`% accuracy for parents and `{r} M_TT_teacher`% accuracy for teachers seems low. 
But.....is it ***abnormally*** low, or do other countries look similar?
